description: Validation gate V1 (mission document §5, §10.1). Anchors are grouped by what they can actually establish. Only the 'independent' tier is capable of failing the model; the gate verdict is computed from that tier alone and is published unrounded, including when it is negative.

authoritativeVolumeSource.rationale: European scope, published by the association of European TSOs, most recent of the candidates (May 2026). Its own figures are a synthesis of IEA 'Energy and AI' (2025), EUDCA 'State of European Data Centres 2025' and an Accenture multi-source consolidation — so it is a secondary source, and it is NOT independent of the IEA anchors above. That is a limitation of the anchor set, recorded here rather than in a footnote.

globalDc2030Twh.label: Global DC demand 2030
globalDc2030Twh.note: Reproduced by construction: k in the logistic is solved so the curve passes through this point. Kept as regression protection; it establishes nothing about the model.

euDcIncrease2024to2030Twh.label: EU-27 DC increase 2024→2030
euDcIncrease2024to2030Twh.note: Reproduced by construction: the EU capture share was set to this anchor (0.085 × (945 − 415) = 45.05).

euDcGrowthRatio2025to2030Min.label: EU-27 DC growth 2025→2030
euDcGrowthRatio2025to2030Min.note: Follows from the same curve as the two anchors above. Retained because it is the one figure ENTSO-E states as a headline, but it cannot fail independently.

europeDc2024Twh.label: Europe DC demand 2024 (base year)
europeDc2024Twh.note: ENTSO-E Figure 1, 'Europe (as total TWh)'. Tests the base year, which no anchor previously checked. Worth reading alongside euDc2024TwhEudca (issue #40): ENTSO-E's 87 TWh is a synthesis that folds in the EUDCA survey (55.3 TWh EU) alongside IEA (~100 TWh EU) and Accenture material, so the two anchors are not independent of each other, and meeting this one is agreement with a midpoint rather than confirmation against either extreme.

europeDc2030TwhMin.label: Europe DC demand 2030
europeDc2030TwhMin.note: ENTSO-E Figure 1 labels this value '2030 (min)'. It is a lower bound, not a central estimate — the model sitting on it is agreement with ENTSO-E's floor, not with its expectation.

europeDc2035TwhMin.label: Europe DC demand 2035
europeDc2035TwhMin.note: ENTSO-E Figure 1, '2035 (min)'; the same figure gives 254 TWh as '2035 (max)'. The lower bound is used, so this is the mildest form of the test.

europeItPower2024Gw.label: Europe installed IT power 2024
europeItPower2024Gw.note: ENTSO-E §1.1: 'over 10,500 data centre facilities across Europe with at least 50 kW of IT power, with capacity totalling approximately 12.7 GW in IT power supply'. Compared against dcItLoadGw, which divides utilisation back out and is therefore an installed-capacity stock, not an average load. Issue #34 established this is an available-IT-power concept (EUDCA 2025 p.22, Fig. 2), not the installed-nominal (Art. 2(14) PD_IT) concept dcItLoadGw represents, and concluded that no re-scoping produced a plausible match. Issue #63 revisited that with a third source and the verdict now has a specific explanation rather than a dead end. The EC Cloud and AI Study (Aug 2026) publishes the exact concept dcItLoadGw computes -- 13.9 GW of 'maximum IT load, assuming 100% utilisation' for the EU-27 in 2025 -- but excludes private enterprise data centres, which the IEA basis this model is anchored on includes. Adding EUDCA's ~2.66 GW of EU-27 enterprise capacity puts the like-for-like figure near 16.6 GW against the model's 19.49 GW: about +18%, not the +80% this anchor reports against ENTSO-E. The residual is NOT a single mis-set parameter. It decomposes into two opposite-signed differences that partly cancel in the capacity figure: the model's EU-27 electricity (72.8 TWh in 2025) sits below the study's 97 TWh, while itUtilization (0.316) sits below the study's stated EU-wide operational average of ~45-50%. Those two utilisation figures are not the same quantity -- ours is drawn power over Art. 2(14) nameplate from mandatory EED reporting (n=770), theirs is an occupancy-style operational rate over commissioned capacity -- which is the same available-vs-installed gap issue #34 named, now visible in a second independent source. Substituting the study's rates would import that mismatch, so itUtilization stays at 0.316. Stays contested: the concept question is resolved, the volume question is not, and the published estimates of European data centre electricity themselves span nearly a factor of two (see europeDc2030TwhEmber at 168 TWh against europeDc2030TwhIea at 109 TWh for the same year and scope).

euItPower2024Gw.label: EU-27 installed IT power 2024
euItPower2024Gw.note: ENTSO-E §1.1 footnote 5: 'Around 9.9 GW of which is in EU27 countries.' Same available-vs-installed-nominal mismatch as europeItPower2024Gw (issue #34), and the same EC Cloud and AI Study cross-check (issue #63) -- see that anchor's note for the decomposition and for why itUtilization is not changed. Moved to contested for the same reason, and stays there.

europeTopFiveSet2024.label: Five largest DC countries 2024
europeTopFiveSet2024.note: ENTSO-E Figure 1 names its countries in rank order; the leading five are taken as a set, because the figure's ordering may follow a projection year rather than 2024.

europeNamedCountrySet2024.label: Countries ENTSO-E names individually
europeNamedCountrySet2024.note: ENTSO-E Figure 1 breaks out these fourteen and aggregates the rest as 'Others'. The model's fourteen largest must be the same fourteen. Tests the allocation module's country distribution, which nothing previously did.

euDcShareOfDemand2030.label: DC share of EU-27 demand 2030
euDcShareOfDemand2030.note: Retained despite coming from a contested source: what it tests is the exogenous demand denominator. An earlier version of this note added 'and Ember's EU demand projection is not the figure ENTSO-E disagrees with' -- that is disproven (issue #68). ENTSO-E's TYNDP 2026 Central Scenario puts EU-27 electricity demand at 2,920 TWh in 2030, while this anchor's share, against the model's own DC volume, implies about 2,490 TWh: a 17% disagreement on exactly that denominator, widening to 25% by 2035. Both readings are now recorded -- see euDemand2030TwhTyndp -- and neither is enforced. Read together with europeDc2030TwhEmber below.

europeDc2030TwhEmber.label: Europe DC demand 2030 — Ember/ICIS reading
europeDc2030TwhEmber.note: Not blocking, because the model follows the designated authority instead. Recorded and published so the disagreement is a stated finding rather than something absorbed by a tolerance.

europeDc2030TwhIea.label: Europe DC demand 2030 — IEA reading
europeDc2030TwhIea.note: The lower end of the published range. Together with the Ember reading it brackets Europe's 2030 DC demand at 109–168 TWh: a 54% spread between published sources, wider than any lever in this model.

euDc2024TwhEudca.label: EU DC demand 2024 — EUDCA reading
euDc2024TwhEudca.note: EUDCA / Pb7 Research, State of European Data Centres 2025: 'approximately 55.3 TWh' EU electricity consumption from data centres, 2023 (issue #40). One year behind the model's 2024 base year; not adjusted for that lag, so the comparison is slightly conservative in the model's favour. Contested rather than independent because the model instead follows ENTSO-E's 87 TWh (europeDc2024Twh, Europe scope) as the designated authority -- but that figure is itself a synthesis that folds in this EUDCA survey alongside IEA and Accenture material, so agreement with ENTSO-E is not independent confirmation against this reading. EUDCA states the disagreement explicitly, in its own footnote: its number is 'significantly lower compared to the most recent IEA estimates for about 100 TWh in 2022', and 'cross checks with non-public data from grid companies show this is in line with their actual data' -- a claim of grid-operator corroboration the IEA figure does not carry. Per EUDCA p.60, the estimate is bottom-up: informal input from grid operators on peak/average capacity usage versus contracted power, plus actual usage data for Denmark, the Netherlands and Ireland, covering 46% of EU colocation-plus-hyperscale by MW -- three of the countries this model treats as connection-constrained.

euDcShareOfDemand2024Eudca.label: DC share of EU electricity demand 2024 — EUDCA
euDcShareOfDemand2024Eudca.note: EUDCA / Pb7 Research: '2% of all electricity usage in the European Union', 2023. Unlike the EU-27 volume anchor above, kept independent rather than contested: EUDCA's estimate has a stated bottom-up basis (grid-operator input plus measured national usage data, p.60 -- see euDc2024TwhEudca's note), which is a different and arguably better-grounded method than the top-down synthesis the ENTSO-E volume anchor rests on, and it is a share, so it is not entangled with the demand-denominator disputes that already run through the 2030 share anchors below (issue #40).

euDc2025TwhEc.label: EU-27 DC electricity 2025 -- EC Cloud & AI study
euDc2025TwhEc.note: EC Study on Cloud and AI Development in the EU (Aug 2026), section 4.3.3.1: 'We estimate data centres in EU27 to consume 97 TWh of electricity in 2025.' Joins the existing disagreement rather than settling it -- the published range for European DC electricity already spanned nearly a factor of two (EUDCA 55.3 TWh EU 2023, IEA ~100 TWh EU 2022, Ember 168 TWh Europe 2030, IEA 109 TWh for the same year and scope), and this reading sits at the high end. Two scope caveats, in opposite directions: the study EXCLUDES private enterprise data centres, which the IEA basis this model follows includes (EUDCA puts EU-27 enterprise capacity near 2.66 GW), so a like-for-like figure would be higher still; but it adds autonomous public-sector capacity that the 12.44 GW commercial fleet figure omits. Contested, not independent: no model can satisfy sources this far apart within a tolerance (issue #63).

euPrimaryMarketShare2025Ec.label: DE/FR/NL/IE share of EU-27 DC 2025 -- EC Cloud & AI study
euPrimaryMarketShare2025Ec.note: EC Study on Cloud and AI Development in the EU (Aug 2026), section 6.5.1: 'roughly 63% of this capacity concentrated in four primary markets (Germany, France, the Netherlands and Ireland)'. The model reproduces this closely without being fitted to it -- the concentration is an output of the gravity/price allocation, not an input -- which makes it the most interesting agreement in the anchor set. Contested rather than independent for two reasons it cannot escape: the study measures a share of CAPACITY where this reads a share of ELECTRICITY (identical in this model, whose PUE and utilisation are single global values, but not in the measured fleet), and the study's denominator excludes private enterprise data centres, which may be distributed differently across countries than colocation and hyperscaler capacity. Recorded so the agreement is visible and so drift in the allocation would surface (issue #63).

euDemand2030TwhTyndp.label: EU-27 total electricity demand 2030 -- TYNDP NT+
euDemand2030TwhTyndp.note: ENTSO-E/ENTSOG TYNDP 2026 Scenarios Report, Central Scenario (National Trends+): EU-27 final electricity demand 'starting from 2,380 TWh in 2023, demand rises to around 2,920 TWh in the short term (2030), reaches 3,710 TWh in the long term (2040)'. Recorded because the model does NOT follow it, despite baselineGrowthPre2030 and baselineGrowthPost2030 having carried this report's source_id since the first commit (issue #68). TYNDP's trajectory implies ~2.5%/yr from 2024; the model's country rates imply ~0.85%/yr. Contested rather than independent because it cannot be met at the same time as euDcShareOfDemand2030 and euDcShareOfDemand2035: those Ember share figures imply an EU-27 denominator of roughly 2,490 TWh in 2030 and 2,684 TWh in 2035, against TYNDP's 2,920 and 3,361 -- a 17% to 25% disagreement between two authorities about the same quantity. Adopting TYNDP's rates was measured: the EU-27 path reproduces the source well (3,789 TWh in 2040), and it takes the gate from 2 to 4 of 8 independent anchors missed and removes the model's only central-run flag. Both readings are therefore recorded and neither is enforced, the same treatment europeDc2030TwhEmber and europeDc2030TwhIea get for the DC volume disagreement. Comparison is against euTotalDemandTwh -- baseline plus data centres -- because TYNDP's demand explicitly includes 'datacentre expansion and cloud-based services'.

euDemand2040TwhTyndp.label: EU-27 total electricity demand 2040 -- TYNDP NT+
euDemand2040TwhTyndp.note: See euDemand2030TwhTyndp for the full note: same source, same disagreement, measured at the later of TYNDP's two published horizons where the gap is widest (issue #68).
